newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK sceptical as Patten denies cover-up in scandal.
newsitem.headline: HK sceptical as Patten denies cover-up in scandal.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten has denied a cover-up but scepticism remained strong in Hong Kong on Thursday over government claims it had ousted its immigration chief because of undisclosed business ties.
Many politicians and analysts were convinced the full story had still to be told, and Patten was likely to face a barrage of questions when he returns from Britain later on Thursday.
Political commentators said the issue was no longer merely restricted to the sins of former Immigration Director Laurence Leung -- the government's own credibility was now on trial.
"Suspicion of a political cover-up in the espisode remains considerable," wrote analyst Chris Yeung in the South China Morning Post newspaper.
Leung's sudden early retirement for "personal reasons" last July caused an uproar in the territory.
British press reports alleged he had been spying for China, which will take over the colony from Britain on July 1 this year after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Leung has denied being a spy.
Patten told reporters in London on Wednesday: "We have got no reason to believe that the integrity or security of the department have been affected over recent years."
But local politicans were not happy with his denial of a cover-up and urged the government to reveal the whole truth.
"We still have our doubts about whether that is the real reason for asking Laurence Leung to leave," Liberal Party leader Allen Lee told the government on Thursday.
"It seems the penalty for his not reporting his dealings or business affairs is quite severe. The government could issue a warning... Nevertheless is that the real reason?" Lee asked.

Last Friday, Leung told a parliamentary inquiry into his sudden departure that he had been forced to quit, contradicting his own and the government's initial stance that he retired for personal reasons.
Leung's about-turn fuelled speculation there were more skeletons in the cupboard.

Lam Woo-kwong, the Hong Kong government's personnel chief, told the Legislative Council inquiry panel on Wednesday that the government had lost confidence in Leung's personal integrity because he did not disclose his business dealings as required.

An anti-corruption probe showed Leung had undisclosed shareholdings, had a business relationship with a legislator, had invested in a mainland Chinese enterprise and had failed to repay a government housing loan promptly, Lam said.

The China-controlled Hong Kong newspaper Ta Kung Pao voiced scepticism about Lam's testimony, saying the real reason for Leung's downfall was probably his close ties with Chinese officials, which explained his abrupt departure.
"Patten's attempt to prevent the dual loyalty of civil servants in the run-up to the handover and only allowing senior civil servants loyal to the Queen is unreasonable," it said.
Lam said allegations of Leung being a China spy were baseless. But he skirted the issue when legislators quizzed him as to whether there were any official reports on Leung alleging security breaches.
"These reports, if existing, are related to the security, confidential matters, and are exempted (from disclosure) because of public interest," he replied to the inquiry panel.
